name: The Hostile Media Effect
statement: Opposing partisans watch the same neutral news report and each side is sure it is biased against them.
statementAccent: each side is sure it is biased against them
meaning: The hostile media effect, or hostile media phenomenon, is a perceptual bias in which partisans on opposing sides of a controversial issue both perceive the same balanced, neutral news coverage as unfairly biased against their own side and in favour of the other. The bias lies in the beholder, not the coverage. It was documented in a 1985 study by Robert Vallone, Lee Ross, and Mark Lepper, who showed pro-Israeli and pro-Arab viewers the same network news coverage of the 1982 Sabra and Shatila massacre in Beirut; each group perceived the identical coverage as biased against their side and predicted it would turn neutral viewers against them. Strikingly, the more knowledgeable partisans were about the conflict, the stronger their perception of bias. The effect helps explain declining trust in media and partisan distrust, and it is a foundational concept in political communication and media-effects research.
mechanism: The effect operates through selective perception and motivated reasoning. Partisans hold strong prior attitudes and believe they know where the truth lies, so they process coverage through that lens. They scrutinise and remember content unfavourable to their side more than favourable content, apply different standards of what counts as fair, and, believing reality favours their position, judge a genuinely balanced presentation as a misrepresentation that shortchanges them. Because both sides do this, each perceives the same neutral report as hostile to itself, evaluating the identical facts differently in light of their divergent views about the merits of the case. A related pattern, the relative hostile media effect, appears when coverage is not perfectly balanced: opposing partisans still perceive it as relatively more favourable to the other side than it is, and partisans may even see objectively slanted coverage as even-handed when the slant targets their opponents. The effect is thus a robust product of how strong prior commitments color the interpretation of media content.

examples.text: Pro-Israeli and pro-Arab viewers of the same 1982 massacre coverage each saw it as biased against their side and expected it to sway neutrals against them.
In the original study, partisans with greater knowledge of the conflict perceived the same coverage as even more biased against their side.
With imperfectly balanced coverage, opposing partisans still see it as relatively more favourable to the other side than it actually is.

variants.name: The relative hostile media effect
variants.text: The version in which partisans perceive imperfectly balanced coverage as more favourable to the opposing side than it is, even when it targets their opponents.

variants.name: Perception versus actual bias
variants.text: The core point that the hostility is in the partisan's perception, not in the coverage, which is neutral.

whyItMatters: The hostile media effect is an important concept in political communication and media-effects research, illuminating why trust in news media has declined and why partisans on all sides so often accuse the press of bias. By showing that opposing partisans perceive the same neutral coverage as hostile to themselves, it reveals that perceived media bias is frequently a product of the audience's prior commitments rather than of actual slant, which complicates efforts to satisfy both sides with balanced reporting. The effect bears directly on polarisation, on the erosion of a shared factual common ground, and on contemporary debates over fake news and partisan distrust of institutions. It stands as a caution that fairness in coverage will not necessarily be perceived as fair, and that the very partisans most engaged with an issue may be the most convinced that the media are against them.

working.text: present opposing partisans with identical, balanced news coverage of a controversial issue.
note that each side sees the same coverage as biased against it, through selective perception and motivated reasoning.

working.lead: Locate the bias in the viewer
working.text: recognise the hostility lies in the partisans' prior commitments, not in the neutral coverage itself.

limits: The hostile media effect concerns perception, not actual media bias, so it does not imply that news coverage is truly neutral in every case; genuine bias can and does exist and must be assessed separately. The effect's strength varies with the intensity of partisanship, the salience of the issue, and how the coverage is framed, and it is most pronounced among strongly committed partisans. Much of the classic evidence comes from particular experimental setups, and some frequently cited details of the original study come from secondary summaries. The related relative hostile media effect broadens the phenomenon to imperfectly balanced coverage but adds complexity about when perceptions track reality.
misreadings: The hostile media effect does not show that media are unbiased or that perceived bias is always illusory; it shows that opposing partisans perceive the same neutral coverage as hostile to themselves, which is about perception, not proof of the coverage's neutrality in general. It is not that one side is right about the bias, since both sides perceive hostility toward themselves from identical content. And it does not deny that real bias exists; it isolates a specific perceptual bias, so treating it as evidence that all complaints of media bias are baseless, or that media are provably fair, overreaches beyond what the effect establishes.
origin: Documented by Robert Vallone, Lee Ross, and Mark Lepper in their 1985 study of partisan perceptions of coverage of the Beirut massacre, showing opposing partisans each saw the same neutral coverage as biased against them.
